title: PVR INOX Bets on ₹175 Tickets to Crack India's Small-Town Cinema Market
excerpt: The multiplex giant's new 'Smart Cinema' format halves construction costs and slashes ticket prices, targeting 300 cities where no quality theatre exists.
body:
• PVR INOX has launched its 'Smart Cinema' format targeting India's tier-2 and tier-3 towns, with tickets priced 30-35% below the national average of ₹254 and construction costs nearly half that of mainstream screens.
  • The company plans 28-30 Smart Cinema screens this fiscal year, with first pilot locations expected by mid-July 2026, as part of a broader push to add 100 smart screens annually.
  • Smart Cinemas will use IoT-based seat locators, vending machines for concessions, and smartphone-enabled ticketing to cut operating costs while maintaining a full multiplex experience.
  • India has fewer than 10,000 cinema screens despite being the world's largest film producer, with only 11.1% of the population visiting theatres — the format targets this massive untapped market.

India's largest multiplex chain is betting that the next wave of cinema growth won't come from luxury lounges in Mumbai or IMAX screens in Delhi, but from ₹175 tickets in towns most urban moviegoers have never heard of. PVR INOX has formally launched its 'Smart Cinema' format — a lean, technology-driven cinema model designed to bring the big-screen experience to India's vast underserved small-town market.

The Economics of Smart Cinema

The numbers behind Smart Cinema tell a clear story of strategic reinvention. A typical PVR INOX screen costs ₹3-4 crore to build, with premium formats running up to ₹5 crore. Smart Cinema screens cost approximately ₹1.9-2.5 crore — nearly half. Ticket prices will run 30-35% below the national average of ₹254, with concession prices similarly reduced.

"We are pursuing a dual-track strategy by expanding our mainstream multiplex business while simultaneously building a new chain of low-priced cinemas."

— Pramod Arora, CEO of Growth & Investment, PVR INOX

The format leverages digital technology to cut operating costs. Concessions will be sold through vending machines, tickets will be smartphone-enabled, and traditional ushers will be replaced with IoT-based seat locators. Each location will be a 3-5 screen setup, smaller than the standard multiplex but designed as a full cinema experience rather than a stripped-down version.

Targeting India's Cinema Desert

The strategic rationale is rooted in India's screen density problem. Despite producing 800-1,200 feature films annually — more than any country in the world — India has fewer than 10,000 cinema screens. Most multiplex infrastructure is concentrated in metros and tier-1 cities, leaving hundreds of millions of potential moviegoers without access to quality theatres.

India had 157 million filmgoers in 2023, up 29% from 122 million in 2022, according to Ormax Media's 'Sizing the Cinema' report. Yet this represented only 11.1% of the population — suggesting enormous headroom for growth if cinema becomes accessible in smaller markets.

PVR INOX currently operates 1,745 screens across 353 cinemas in 111 cities in India and Sri Lanka. The company's mainstream cinema count fell 2.5% to 352 in the first quarter, while its screen count slipped 0.6% to 1,743, underscoring the need for new growth vectors.

The Roll-Out Plan

The first wave of Smart Cinema deployments will target North India, including Uttar Pradesh, and towns in the northeast. The company is targeting 28-30 Smart Cinema screens this fiscal year, with the first pilot locations expected to open by mid-July 2026. The long-term target is 100 smart screens annually, on top of the existing expansion target of 100-120 mainstream screens each year.

Funding will follow multiple models: company-owned, franchisee-owned company-operated, and asset-light developer partnerships. The franchise model allows PVR INOX to expand with reduced financial risk, contributing less capital than the developer while retaining full operational control and earning revenue through profit-sharing instead of fixed rentals.

What It Means for Bollywood and Beyond

For India's film industry, Smart Cinema represents a potential step-change in distribution reach. Regional films in languages like Bhojpuri, Marathi, and Assamese that rarely find multiplex screens in metros could gain dedicated exhibition space in their home markets. The increased screen count could also support Bollywood's growing slate of mid-budget films that struggle to compete for limited screens against tentpole releases.

For NRI investors, PVR INOX's Smart Cinema pivot mirrors a broader trend of Indian consumer businesses finding scalable models for the country's tier-2 and tier-3 markets — the same dynamic driving growth at companies from DMart to Jio.
